title: Gravitational Fields, Satellites and Orbits
seo_title: Year 12 Physics: Gravitational Fields and Orbits Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Newton's law of universal gravitation; gravitational field strength and its variation with distance; satellite motion and orbital speed and period; geostationary orbits; Kepler's laws. (Senior Secondary Physics, Unit 3: Gravity and electromagnetism)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Physics worksheets on gravity: Newton's law of gravitation, field strength, orbital speed and period, geostationary orbits and Kepler's third law. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: For orbits: v = √(GM/r) and T² ∝ r³.
body_html:
How to think about it

Every mass attracts every other mass: F = GMm ÷ r², with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². The gravitational field strength g = GM ÷ r² falls with the square of the distance from the centre.

For a satellite, gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r) and T = 2πr/v. Lower orbits are faster. Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³. A geostationary satellite orbits above the Equator with T = 24 h.

Example

Distance doubles. New force?

F ∝ 1/r²

(1/2)² = 1/4

Answer: one quarter

Example

Planet with r 4 times Earth's (1 AU). Period?

T² = 4³ = 64

Answer: 8 years

Common mistakes

  • Using the height above the surface instead of the distance from the centre.
  • Thinking there is no gravity in orbit.
  • Saying a heavier satellite needs a faster orbital speed.

faq.q: Why do astronauts float in the ISS?
faq.a: They are in free fall together with the station; gravity there is still about 90% of its surface value.

faq.q: Does the orbital speed depend on the satellite's mass?
faq.a: No: v = √(GM/r) depends only on the planet's mass and the orbit radius.
